memo: Hand-curated research pack (verified 2026-10-15 by reading the primary sources). Sugiyama et al. 2008 (New J. Phys. 10 033001, CC BY 4.0): 22 vehicles on a 230 m circular road; drivers requested to cruise at about 30 km/h with near-uniform spacing; 'even a tiny fluctuation grows larger and then the homogeneous movement cannot be maintained'; a jam cluster appears and propagates backward; the cluster travels backward at roughly 20 km/h, 'the common value of the velocity of a jam measured on real highways'; title claim: jams without bottlenecks - a bottleneck is a trigger, not the essential origin. Empirical highway studies: stop-and-go waves propagate upstream at about -15 +/- 5 km/h (Schoenhof & Helbing, cond-mat/0408138); Kerner et al. (1012.5160) report about -14.5 to -17 km/h on German, US and UK freeways. Stern et al. 2018 (Transp. Res. C 89, arXiv 1705.01693): ring experiments with 20+ vehicles - waves emerge consistently and can be dampened by controlling the velocity of a single (autonomous) vehicle. Caveats: jams do not form at every density - the ring density was chosen to be in the unstable regime; a single brake tap does not inevitably create a jam.
